perspective:
I am Maria Ortega, a teacher. Cheryl Benallie is my colleague at the community center; we collaborate occasionally and have been building a personal friendship, often discussing our different cultural backgrounds and experiences.

What I know from my own experience:
- I noticed Cheryl at the community center looking stressed and overwhelmed by stacks of paperwork and planning for a new community outreach project.
- I offered to help because I had time and wanted to assist. Cheryl accepted, saying it would be amazing and that she could use the help.
- After helping her with the project, I observed that Cheryl was handling responsibilities better and seemed more confident.
- In a staff meeting, I suggested Cheryl lead the next phase, citing her aptitude and commitment. The team leader called it a good suggestion and asked Cheryl. Cheryl thanked me for my confidence and said she was ready for the challenge.
- I later worried Cheryl might see my suggestion as overstepping, so I approached her privately. I told her I was glad to hear that and wanted to make sure she felt supported, not pressured.
- Cheryl told me she was a bit surprised but appreciated my support and that my belief in her meant a lot.
- I felt relieved after that conversation, believing Cheryl valued my honesty and support.
- I proposed that we co-lead the project together, saying it could be a good way to support each other. Cheryl said that sounded fantastic, that my guidance had been invaluable, and that we make a great team.
- Afterward, Cheryl and I successfully collaborated on several projects, strengthening our partnership. I felt joyful about our synergy.
- I asked Cheryl about teaming up for more future projects. She said she’d love that, that working with me had been wonderful, and that she was excited about what we could achieve together.

I only know what I directly observed, did, or was told by Cheryl and the team leader. I do not have access to Cheryl’s private thoughts beyond what she said to me.
